candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight. The partnership is composed of seven members: Belgium, Luxembourg, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom, NATO headquarters, and now Ukraine. Following approval by Allies in the North Atlantic Council (NAC) in April 2026, NSPA are able to issue solicitations and sign contracts with Ukrainian industry. NSPA led a dedicated Ukraine Industry Day in Kyiv on October 14, with 150 Ukrainian companies in attendance. It was a first-of-its-kind event by a NATO organization since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. However, its point of greatest eclipse occurs just a few miles from Thebes, the magnificent religious and political capital of ancient Egypt's Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom. On the east bank of the mighty Nile is Luxor, the great city of the living, with its massive temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor. On its west bank is the city of the dead, which includes the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Hatshepsut. Modern Luxor, population 285,000, is set to become a focal point for eclipse chasers on Aug. 2, 2027, and will attract many thousands of international visitors. They'll come for the forecasted 0% chance of clouds and the era-defining duration of totality, but also to tour ancient Egypt's temples and monuments. The chances of actually witnessing totality at any of the major temples are probably slim. Still, almost every eclipse chaser headed to Luxor will want to tour them before or after the eclipse. Visitors should be prepared for extreme August heat and check official opening and access arrangements before planning to watch the eclipse at any archaeological site. Certified eclipse glasses are essential during the partial phases; only during totality, when the sun is completely covered, is it safe to look without them. According to Naja, the failed test took place on 6 October, when the test model was released from a helicopter at an altitude of approximately three kilometres over a military test range in Sardinia, Italy. candidates.title: Australia's bizarre 'Spider Crater' seen from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 22, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one. What is it? One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said . In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape. Complete with "legs," the planetary imprint has earned its name Spider Crater. This image shows the impact structure in its entirety, which stretches 8 by 7 miles (13 by 11 kilometers) in full, with the central "spider" piece measuring 2.5 miles (4 km). Why is it incredible? In this image, we can see this "spider" from space. This snapshot shows the geologic feature as captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the Landsat 9 satellite , an Earth-observing craft that launched back in 2021. The satellite, a collaborative effort between NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey, is the ninth in the Landsat Earth-observing series, which goes all the way back to the launch of Landsat 1 in 1972. On a near-weekly basis, Landsat 9 delivers observations of everything from deforestation to water quality and crop growth. The series of Landsat satellites have been a critical piece in the modern understanding of how our planet continues to change. Whether it's the repercussions of climate change or fluctuations in agriculture, observations from orbit do more than provide interesting photos of our home world; they also capture critical data.

candidates.title: Anthropic’s Financial Situation May Explain Why Dario Amodei Looks So Terrified All the Time
candidates.raw_excerpt: Pull up any random photo of billionaire Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and you’re likely to land on a facial expression expressing something between horror and deep consternation. There may be a simple explanation for that: he knows the truth about his company’s finances. New reporting by the Wall Street Journal revealed the mounting costs for the AI lab, which ballooned to a net loss of $80 billion in the first six months of 2026. Anthropic’s losses for the same period a year prior were $13 billion — still an eye-watering sum, but peanuts compared to its runaway spending this year (the WSJ called it “one of the largest half-year losses ever reported.”) The bleak financial numbers come from a draft IPO prospectus viewed by the WSJ , which notes that the company’s revenue for the first half of 2026 grew by just $1.1 billion over the same period to $16.3 billion. The figures add to the anxiety around how long the AI spending bubble can sustain itself. If Anthropic’s losses continue to mount at a rate far exceeding revenue growth, there’s simply no way the lab can dig itself out of the hole it’s burrowed for itself. That would be bad news for the US economy as a whole, which now hinges almost entirely on circular AI investments and data center development . Beyond the immediate losses, the WSJ notes that the AI lab is also footing a $450 billion bill for cloud computing infrastructure over the next seven to ten years — meaning the clock is ticking on what is surely the costliest game of “kick-the-can” the world has ever seen. NASA asked the committee which science goals in locations beyond the poles need people rather than robots, and where to send those astronauts. The committee’s answer assumes short sorties: two-person crews, no rover, and one to four moonwalks per site. Sites were weighed on three criteria: whether science aligned with the decadal surveys and NASA’s Moon to Mars objectives, if the missions would expand US exploration capabilities, and, to a lesser degree, how they would contribute to public inspiration. Site seeing: The sites, in priority order: Bhabha Crater: Astronauts have never landed this far from Earth. The far-side crater sits in the middle of the South Pole-Aitken Basin, which may have the oldest impact signature in the solar system. The region is also shielded from Earth’s radio noise, making it a prime spot for low-frequency astronomy. Mons Hadley: Apollo 11 and 17 are seen by NASA as protected heritage sites because of their historical significance, so the committee picked the Apollo 15 site instead. Crews would land ~2 km away from the Apollo site and venture over to investigate how the hardware and astronaut waste left behind have held up after 55+ years. Orientale Basin: It’s the Moon’s youngest large impact basin—and best-preserved. Boulders that tumbled off the region’s inner mountain rings could give scientists their first look at the deep lunar crust. As launches get more common and rockets get larger and sturdier — the model built by LandSpace, which deposited the debris in the cornfield, is a workhorse spacecraft meant to ferry cargo to Earth’s orbit — the chances of their detritus surviving the journey back to the ground increases. These chunks of spacefaring equipment can sometimes crash down in populated areas. In 2024, a NASA component from the International Space Station withstood reentry and crashed through a home in Florida where a family was sleeping. Space wreckage has previously been discovered previously on farms in Canada and Australia . Nobody has yet been injured by a piece of falling space debris, but as commercial ambitions for Earth’s orbit increase — the Chinese rocket had been launched to deploy satellites for a connectivity constellation meant to rival SpaceX’s Starlink — it’s probably only a matter of time. candidates.title: Orionid meteor shower peaks tonight: Here's the best time to spot shooting stars
candidates.raw_excerpt: Don't miss the Orionid meteor shower peak tonight (Oct. 21-22) as tiny shards of Halley's Comet collide with Earth's atmosphere to carve fiery streaks through the Autumn sky! But will the light cast by the waxing gibbous moon spoil the show? The Orionid meteor shower activity peaks when Earth travels through the densest section of the debris trail left by Comet 1P/Halley. The comet is currently racing back towards the sun ahead of its next visit to the inner solar system in 2061. Under perfect dark sky conditions 10 to 20 shooting stars could brighten the night sky each hour as the peak unfolds, according to NASA . However, the light cast by the waxing moon — just four days from being full — will likely reduce the number of visible meteors by hiding fainter Orionids from sight. Orionid shooting stars will appear to travel away from a point of origin, close to the red star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion , rising above the eastern horizon an hour before midnight for viewers in the U.S. When and where to see Orionid shooting stars this October Your best chance at spotting the fast-moving meteors will come in the hours before dawn on Oct. 22, after the moon has set and the radiant approaches its highest point in the night sky. It's best not to stare directly at the radiant, where the glowing meteor trails will be relatively short compared to those left by shooting stars that appear 45-90 degrees away from the bright star Betelgeuse, thanks to an effect known as foreshortening. China's experience in biodiversity conservation offers valuable lessons for the world, particularly in combining ambitious commitments with sound science, effective institutions and long-term investment, the UN biodiversity chief said on Monday.

China's experience is particularly evident in the scale of its conservation efforts and its integration of biodiversity into national development planning, Schomaker said.

Its ecological conservation redline system, national parks network, ecological restoration programs and investments in biodiversity monitoring demonstrate practical approaches to implementing national commitments, she said.

In her eyes, three lessons stand out from China's experience: conservation must be integrated into broader economic and land-use planning; ecological restoration requires sustained investment; and effective monitoring is essential to measuring results.

China's contribution extends beyond its domestic efforts. "Its continued support for multilateral cooperation is especially valuable amid today's geopolitical challenges," Schomaker said.

candidates.raw_excerpt:
A CERES-1S Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 am Beijing time on Wednesday from waters near east China's Shandong Province, delivering the Xiguang-4 01 satellite into a 541 km-altitude low Earth orbit.

Xiguang-4 01 is the pilot satellite of the Wuyang Constellation, the world's first low-inclination remote sensing constellation. After entering orbit, Xiguang-4 01 will mainly provide commercial remote sensing services for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, South China, and low-latitude regions along the Maritime Silk Road. Its support functions will include natural resource monitoring, agricultural production, marine observation, ecological protection, flood and typhoon emergency response, disaster mitigation and urban governance.

Developed by Galactic Energy, the CERES-1 rocket model is China's first commercial rocket model capable of launching from both land and sea platforms. Wednesday's launch was the seventh sea launch mission of the CERES-1S carrier rocket. Since its maiden flight on September 5, 2023, the CERES-1S has maintained a 100% launch success rate.

candidates.title: China to build world's first deep-sea floating island
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China is to build the world's first floating artificial island for all-weather, long-term deep-sea scientific research. Under a contract signed in Shanghai, the project will be undertaken by Shanghai Jiao Tong University and constructed by Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), the world's largest shipbuilding group.

As the world's first ultra-large marine scientific research platform, the artificial island is being designed to withstand extreme sea conditions and maintain long-term presence in the open ocean, while also offering rapid mobility and deployment. It will serve as a research base for frontier studies in marine science, marine equipment, and marine meteorology.

The large scientific facility will comprise three main systems: the main facility platform, ship-based laboratories, and shore-based support. The main facility platform will have a "semi-submersible twin-hull" design. It will be 138 meters long, 85 meters wide, with a main deck height of 45 meters. It's set to sustain sea state 7 conditions and safely survive a category 17 typhoon.

The order to build the facility is worth 2.76 billion yuan (about 413 million US dollars). Developed as a national major science and technology infrastructure project, Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding is expected to begin construction in 2028, with delivery due in June, 2030.

candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program. After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars , the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind. The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon , but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems. Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth. The spacecraft still returned to Earth safely and splashed down in the Indian Ocean one week after it launched. The Soviet Union's Zond 8 spacecraft, the last in a series of lunar spacecraft, captured this image of Earthrise on Oct. 24, 1970. (Image credit: Moscow State University of Geodesy and Cartography) Why it mattered While the Zond 1 and Zond 2 missions were launched toward Venus and Mars, respectively, the primary target of most Zond missions was the moon. At the time, the Soviet Union was embroiled in an ongoing space race with the United States to be the first on the moon with a human crew. By the time Zond 8 launched on Oct. 20, 1970, that space race was lost to the Soviet Union. NASA and the U.S. had already landed astronauts on the moon twice with Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 (in July and November of 1969, respectively), and even peformed the first space rescue fo the Apollo 13 astronauts in April 1970. While Zond 8 was uncrewed, it was a test flight of the Soviet Union's L1 spacecraft that was designed to fly a cosmonaut around the moon. We are pleased to welcome Nvidia among our investors as we continue to scale production to meet growing demand.” Nvidia announced investments into four German startups this week during the Invest in Germany Summit. Nvidia also invested in AI robot company Agile Robots, healthcare tech startup Avelios Medical, Mirelo, an AI startup for audio production. candidates.title: Four Democratic Senators Ask SpaceX for Answers on Starshield Restrictions
candidates.raw_excerpt: Four Senate Democrats are seeking insights from SpaceX on the degradation of the company’s military Starshield system for Ukraine. On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials reported a lack of access to Starshield and its commercial counterpart, Starlink, for host systems traveling more than 100 miles per hour. Ukraine has had particular need for such systems in the effort to counter the advent of Russian jet-powered one way attack drones, such as the Geran-4 and Geran-5. “This [speed] restriction was particularly devastating to the Ukrainian military’s drone capabilities during an ongoing Russian bombing campaign in Kyiv,” according to a Monday letter to Christopher Cardaci, SpaceX’s counsel, from Senators Christopher Coons, D-Del., the ranking Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee’s defense subcommittee; Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the second ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC); Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., another SASC member; and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I. While SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said that responsibility for the Starshield and Starlink restrictions lies with the White House, not his company. “These circumstances raise important questions about the respective technical, contractual, and operational authorities retained by SpaceX and the U.S. government, as well as the ability SpaceX has to restrict access to either Starshield or Starlink services during military operations or national security emergencies,” according to the senators’ letter. By Nov. 2, the senators want responses from SpaceX on a number of questions, including all U.S. government/SpaceX communications that led to the restriction and the date when SpaceX notified the German government of the restrictions, as Germany funds Ukraine’s access to Starlink. SpaceX launched the mission on a Falcon 9 rocket early on Tuesday, lifting off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 7:04 a.m. ET. Planet Labs flew one Pelican satellite onboard the mission. In addition, SES Space & Defense flew a demonstration payload on Pelican-12 satellite for NASA ’s Communications Services Project (CSP). candidates.title: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
candidates.raw_excerpt: It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded. The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets , spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. Bezos founded Blue Origin in 2000. Because he has financed so much of its development by himself , the company has been able to pursue ambitious engineering projects without the financial pressures that publicly listed businesses typically face. Bezos, then, has good reasons to seek additional sources of investment — particularly as Blue Origin prepares to expand its commercial operations. candidates.title: A supercomputer is about to launch to the moon aboard a rover named FLIP
candidates.raw_excerpt: HAWTHORNE, Calif. — A moon buggy carrying a history-making supercomputer is ready to launch to the lunar surface. And it's taking some inspiration from Mars. Later this year, Astrolab will launch its uncrewed moon rover FLIP to the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1, or Griffin-1. The California company is one of two that NASA has selected to develop a drivable rover for the agency's Artemis program. On board FLIP will be Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4, an advanced computer module built to be used in space. This will be the first time that high-performance computing and artificial intelligence will be tested on the lunar surface. As NASA gets closer to landing humans back on the moon with Artemis, advancements like this aim to support future human habitation as well as economic activity on and around the moon. "We're sending the first supercomputer from HPE to the lunar surface later this year, doing the first GPU [graphics processing unit] on the moon [and the] first AI experiments on the moon," Jaret Matthews, founder and CEO of Astrolab, said during an Oct. 14 media event here at Astrolab's headquarters. "They're breaking new ground, and they're ahead of the curve." The computer is designed to be lightweight, compact, self-contained and fanless. It has a low-power 64-bit CPU (central processing unit) with a GPU. The computer will be attached to FLIP's cooling system and will be powered by a system supported by both batteries and solar cells on the rover. The computer will also be paired with solid state drives from the company KIOXIA that will allow for memory storage. Mission Control at Astrolab.
